title: What Do Emissions Markets Deliver and to Whom? Evidence from Southern California's NOx Trading Program
research_question: Does replacing prescriptive emissions regulations with a market-based cap-and-trade program for nitrogen oxides reduce facility-level emissions beyond what would have occurred under the prior regulatory regime? And does the compliance flexibility afforded by such a market-based approach lead to disproportionate pollution outcomes in low-income or minority neighborhoods relative to more prescriptive regulation?
data_description: The primary data come from the California Air Resources Board (ARB) emissions database, which compiles facility-level reports of criteria pollutant emissions (focusing on NOx) from local Air Quality Management Districts for roughly 10,000 polluting facilities in California. Emissions are observed annually from 1990 through 2005 and aggregated into four periods: 1990-1993 (pre-program), 1997-1998, 2001-2002, and 2004-2005. Facility records include addresses, geocodes, and 4-digit SIC industry classifications (available from 1990). Separate facility-level NOx allocation and quarterly emissions data from the South Coast Air Quality Management District (SCAQMD) are used to verify ARB reports, and RECLAIM Trading Credit price data come from Evolution Markets LLC. Zip-code-level demographic variables (median household income in 1999, racial/ethnic composition) are drawn from the 2000 Census Summary File 3, and census-tract centroids within 0.5, 1, and 2 miles of facilities are used to compute exposure measures. The unit of observation is the industrial facility-period.
institutional_context: The setting is air pollution regulation in non-attainment areas of California during the 1990s and 2000s. Under the 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments, extreme ozone non-attainment regions were required to adopt economic incentive programs to meet federal ambient air quality standards. In response, the South Coast Air Quality Management District (covering the Los Angeles basin) replaced more than 40 prescriptive command-and-control rules with the Regional Clean Air Incentives Market (RECLAIM), a cap-and-trade program for NOx and SO2 launched in 1994. Participation was mandatory for SCAQMD facilities emitting at least four tons per year of NOx or SO2; smaller emitters within SCAQMD and facilities elsewhere in California's non-attainment counties remained under the prior prescriptive regime. The aggregate NOx cap declined steeply over time, became binding around 1999-2000, and experienced a sharp permit price spike during the 2000-2001 California electricity crisis, prompting amendments that separated 14 power producers from the trading market.

key_variables.treatment: participation in the NOx trading program

key_variables.outcome: NOx emissions levels, firm economic performance
key_variables.time_period: years before and after the program implementation

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The implementation of the NOx trading program led to a reduction in emissions and had positive economic effects on participating firms.
